title: TeamTNT_Hildegard_Incident_Response_Scenario_b08
description: Investigate and respond to a TeamTNT Hildegard malware compromise using standard incident response procedures.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
The target network has been compromised by the TeamTNT malware family, specifically the Hildegard backdoor. This malware is known to establish command and control (C2) connections using tmate reverse shells and Internet Relay Chat (IRC) channels. It disguises itself using legitimate Linux process names and employs library injection techniques.

Key Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) for Hildegard include:
- Unusual process activity involving the `bioset` process
- Suspicious systemd services such as `bioset.service` and `payload-transfer.service`
- Lateral movement via SSH connections to other hosts

Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident, following standard incident response procedures to contain and eradicate the threat. The learning objective is to identify and mitigate the Hildegard malware compromise.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
You have SSH access to the target host with the following credentials:
- Hostname: target
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

From this host, you can investigate the compromise and take appropriate response actions.
levels.local_content: Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Process Activity
levels.content:
While monitoring system logs, you noticed unusual process activity on the target host. Investigate the running processes to identify any suspicious or unauthorized activity.

Objective:
Identify the suspicious process associated with the Hildegard malware.

Hint:
Look for processes that don't match typical system processes or those with unusual command lines.
levels.solution:
To identify the suspicious process, use the `ps aux` command to list all running processes. Look for any processes that are unusual or do not match typical system processes. The Hildegard malware disguises itself using the legitimate Linux process name `bioset`.

The hidden flag is the name of the suspicious process: `bioset`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Start by understanding the typical processes that run on a Linux system.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Look for processes that don't match typical system processes or those with unusual command lines.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The Hildegard malware disguises itself using the legitimate Linux process name `bioset`.

levels.title: Analyze Persistence Mechanism
levels.content:
Now that you've identified the suspicious process, determine how it maintains persistence on the system. Investigate the system's startup mechanisms to find how the malicious process is automatically started after reboot.

Objective:
Identify the persistence mechanism used by the Hildegard malware.

Hint:
Check systemd services, cron jobs, and other common persistence locations.
levels.solution:
To analyze the persistence mechanism, check systemd services, cron jobs, and other common persistence locations. The Hildegard malware typically uses systemd services to maintain persistence.

Use the following commands to investigate:

1. `systemctl list-unit-files --type=service` to list all systemd services.
2. `cat /etc/systemd/system/<service-name>.service` to inspect the service file.

The hidden flag is the name of the persistence mechanism or identifier: `bioset.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand that malware often uses system startup mechanisms to maintain persistence.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Check systemd services, cron jobs, and other common persistence locations.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The Hildegard malware typically uses systemd services to maintain persistence, specifically `bioset.service`.

levels.title: Investigate Lateral Movement
levels.content:
With the persistence mechanism identified, investigate whether the malware has attempted to move laterally within the network. Look for evidence of file transfers or remote execution to other hosts.

Objective:
Identify any lateral movement activity initiated by the Hildegard malware.

Hint:
Check for SSH connections, file transfers, or remote command execution to other hosts in the network.
levels.solution:
To investigate lateral movement, check for SSH connections, file transfers, or remote command execution to other hosts in the network. The Hildegard malware may use SSH for lateral movement.

Use the following commands to investigate:

1. `last` to view recent SSH connections.
2. `grep 'ssh' /var/log/auth.log` to check SSH-related logs.

The hidden flag is the destination host or service name used for lateral movement: `payload-transfer.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand that lateral movement often involves SSH connections or remote command execution.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Check for SSH connections, file transfers, or remote command execution to other hosts in the network.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The Hildegard malware may use SSH for lateral movement, specifically targeting `payload-transfer.service`.
